The backup energy source (generators and/or BESS) are connected at a low voltage in some designs (such as in Figure 1 (a), (b), (c), (e)) and at the medium-voltage level in others (Figure 1 (d) and (f)). The UPS helps keep the IT hardware powered when the data center transitions from utility power to a backup source (generator power) during a utility outage. A recent PJM event called on dispatching on-site generators in hyperscale data centers to serve the grid. Such changes in operational requirements require modifications at the physical hardware level (possibly higher ratings of switchgear) as well as modifications of the controls software. In short, this is riskier to implement in brownfield sites. • BESS: Recently, owing to grid capacity constraints, data centers are increasingly being considered for grid services such as demand response. A recent report from EPRI (2025) compares the different approaches for data center load flexibility; in the report, BESS are particularly suitable compared to generators because of both reliability and emission constraints. In Figure 1 (f), the system design from Verrus accounts for grid paralleling of the BESS to respond to demand response requests (Vaidhynathan et al. 2025) through appropriate control systems. • Cooling load: The cooling system in data centers comprises pumps, chillers, air handling units, and coolant distribution units, which are low-voltage loads (~400–480 V). Many of these have variable-frequency drives. In most data centers, the IT and cooling loads are separate power distribution systems (see Figure 1 (a) to (e); cooling systems are not included), unlike the design from Verrus shown in Figure 1 (f), where cooling loads and IT loads are fed from the common medium-voltage bus. Appropriate backup power systems are put in place for cooling loads to meet the uptime requirements of the data center. In recent times, cooling systems in data centers are being considered for load flexibility (EPRI 2025) and power usage effectiveness optimization (Lazic et al. 2018). Most traditional data center design and operational philosophies cater only to the uptime, inherently leading to data centers being a passive participant on the grid. The operations must keep the IT hardware operating 24-7, which can sometimes exacerbate grid instability during voltage events (as described in the NERC incident review [NERC 2025]) based on the protection schemes implemented on the load side. The NERC incident review found almost 1,500 MW of data center load disconnecting from the grid during approximate 10-millisecond-scale grid-side faults, causing overvoltages and overfrequencies on the grid, with the possibility of causing a wide-area outage.
